title: verify_ocsp_responder takes &Certificate for issuer but doesn't enforce that it's in the chain
description: pkix-chain/src/lib.rs:1235-1279: verify_ocsp_responder takes `issuer: &Certificate` AND `chain: &[Certificate]`. The two arguments must be consistent (chain[0].issuer matches issuer.subject by DN, AND ideally issuer is in the chain so verify_chain's signature check covers it) but the function does NOT enforce that issuer is in chain. The rustdoc at lines 1286-1290 hand-waves: 'The cryptographic signature check ... is already covered by verify_chain when issuer appears in the chain.' But the function doesn't VERIFY that issuer appears in chain — a caller can pass a completely orphan `issuer` cert that DN-matches chain[0].issuer without ever being in the chain or anchors. Then the wrapper returns Ok even though the supposed-issuer never signed anything. This is closely related to PKIX-q9hv.3 (DN-match insufficient). Two layers of fix: (a) the spec-correct delegation pinning per PKIX-q9hv.3, AND (b) enforce that `issuer` either appears in chain (by content equality) or is the trust anchor that terminated the path. Otherwise the issuer argument is API-level theater.
notes:
Analysis 2026-11-25: the headline claim is now FALSE, so this is no longer a P1. Dropped to P2 with the residual item recorded rather than closed.

The bead says "the wrapper returns Ok even though the supposed-issuer never signed anything" and asks for two fixes.

Fix (a) -- spec-correct delegation pinning, tracked as q9hv.3 -- IS DONE. verify_responder_is_delegated_by (lib.rs:1456) does two things: a DN gate via names_match, then a cryptographic check that chain[0].signature verifies under issuer SPKI over the re-encoded TBSCertificate. So the issuer provably signed the responder cert; an orphan cert that merely DN-matches is rejected. The premise of the bead no longer holds.

Fix (b) -- enforce issuer appears in chain or is the terminating anchor -- is now largely redundant, and not free. Reasoning: for the chain to validate, chain[0] must be signed by its in-chain parent or the anchor; for the delegation check to pass, issuer SPKI must verify chain[0] signature. Both conditions together mean issuer must carry the same public key as the certificate that actually signed the responder. Adding content equality would reject only a DIFFERENT certificate bearing the SAME key -- a cross-certificate or a same-key renewal -- which is a legitimate configuration, not an attack.

An attacker cannot exploit the gap to change the answer: to pass both gates a forged issuer must carry the real CA subject DN and the real CA public key, which is that CA identity. Public keys are public, so minting such a certificate is possible and pointless -- it conveys the same (DN, key) pair the caller asked about.

Residual, and the reason this stays open at P2: issuer itself is never path-validated, so its own validity window, revocation status and basicConstraints are unchecked. A caller passing an expired or revoked issuer gets Ok. That is a real if modest gap -- the delegation is proven against an unvalidated certificate. Worth a rustdoc note stating the caller obligation, which is cheaper and less likely to break legitimate same-key topologies than enforcing chain membership.

Related and now closed: PKIX-sqek.9, which concerned the same function hardcoding DefaultVerifier for this very binding instead of using the caller verifier.
